name: Dynamic Array Usage
description: Use ArrayList or vector-style indexed storage, resizing expectations, and linear traversal habits confidently in DSA code.
exampleJava: for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) nums[i] += nums[i - 1];
commonMistakes: Rebuilding arrays unnecessarily instead of updating in place
Mixing index math and loop boundaries

name: String Builder Usage
description: Use StringBuilder or mutable string accumulation patterns instead of slow repeated immutable concatenation.
commonMistakes: Concatenating immutable strings inside long loops
Forgetting to append the leftover suffix after one string ends

name: Hash Map Usage
description: Use HashMap or unordered_map style counting and lookup patterns to model frequencies, presence checks, and stored intermediate answers.
commonMistakes: Reading a missing key without a default value
Updating only one side of a frequency comparison

name: Frequency Map Basics
description: Count characters or values with a map so repeated elements can be compared, ranked, or validated.
commonMistakes: Incrementing counts for only one side of a comparison
Forgetting that zero-count entries can be removed or ignored

name: Seen-Set Membership
description: Use a set when you only need to know whether something has appeared before.
commonMistakes: Using a full frequency map when only membership is needed
Forgetting that add returning false usually means the value already existed

name: Value-to-Index Mapping
description: Store the earliest or most useful index for each value so future positions can answer questions in O(1).
commonMistakes: Overwriting the first useful index accidentally
Storing values when the later logic really needs positions

name: Stack Library Usage
description: Use stack-like library operations cleanly for push, pop, peek, and last-kept-element simulation.
exampleJava: if (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() == ch) stack.pop(); else stack.push(ch);
commonMistakes: Popping without checking emptiness
Using the wrong end of the container as the top

name: Queue Library Usage
description: Use queue-style APIs for FIFO processing, front access, and query simulation without shifting full arrays manually.
commonMistakes: Using remove(0) on a dynamic array instead of a queue structure
Confusing front and rear operations

name: Deque Library Usage
description: Use both ends of a deque intentionally for front expiry, back cleanup, and double-ended query simulation.
commonMistakes: Calling queue-style operations when the logic needs both ends
Mixing value expiry with index expiry

name: Monotonic Deque Usage
description: Keep deque entries in monotonic order so the best candidate is always ready at the front.
commonMistakes: Storing values when positions are needed for expiry
Forgetting to remove expired indices before reading the answer

name: Priority Queue Usage
description: Use min-heaps or max-heaps correctly for top-k and best-first maintenance patterns.
commonMistakes: Choosing a max-heap when the pattern needs a min-heap of size k
Forgetting to evict elements when the heap grows past the intended size

name: Heap Top-K Usage
description: Maintain only the best K values in a heap instead of repeatedly sorting the whole collection.
exampleJava: if (heap.size() < k) heap.offer(value); else if (value > heap.peek()) { heap.poll(); heap.offer(value); }
commonMistakes: Keeping all elements in the heap when the pattern only needs K
Using the wrong heap direction for top-k vs bottom-k

name: Tokenization Usage
description: Break a sentence into words or chunks while handling boundaries and separators carefully.
commonMistakes: Treating repeated spaces as real empty tokens
Losing the last token because the scan stops too early

name: String Normalization Usage
description: Clean spacing, casing, or accumulated formatting so later logic works on a consistent string shape.
commonMistakes: Keeping leading or trailing spaces in the final result
Normalizing too aggressively and losing required characters

name: Collection Iteration Usage
description: Move comfortably between arrays, strings, maps, sets, queues, deques, and heaps while keeping loops and temporary state under control.
exampleJava: for (int value : nums) { if (heap.size() < k) heap.offer(value); }
commonMistakes: Nesting extra loops because container traversal feels unfamiliar
Using incompatible container operations for the required access pattern

name: Sorting Helper Usage
description: Use built-in sorting helpers cleanly on arrays, lists, or strings before more advanced comparator-based patterns.
commonMistakes: Sorting when the original order was supposed to stay intact
Forgetting to convert between containers before sorting

name: Pair Collection Usage
description: Store and iterate over value pairs cleanly when problems need a key plus metadata like frequency, index, or distance.
exampleJava: List<int[]> pairs = new ArrayList<>(); pairs.add(new int[] {value, frequency});
commonMistakes: Losing track of which slot stores which meaning
Using parallel arrays when a paired representation is simpler

name: Comparator Sorting Usage
description: Sort pairs or objects by a custom priority such as frequency, index, or multiple tie-break rules.
exampleJava: pairs.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
commonMistakes: Applying the tie-break in the wrong direction
Sorting the right data but forgetting the intended priority order

name: Map Iteration Order Usage
description: Know when plain hash map iteration order is irrelevant and when you need explicit sorting or an ordered map strategy.
exampleJava: for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> entry : counts.entrySet()) ordered.add(new int[] {entry.getKey(), entry.getValue()});
commonMistakes: Assuming a hash map iterates in sorted order
Returning entries in arbitrary order when the output requires ordering

name: Ordered Map Usage
description: Use a TreeMap or ordered map pattern when keys must be processed in sorted order without a separate full sort step.
commonMistakes: Using a hash map and then being surprised by arbitrary key order
Paying an unnecessary sorting cost when an ordered map would simplify the flow

name: Heap of Pairs Usage
description: Use a priority queue of pairs when each candidate has both a payload and a priority such as distance, frequency, or timestamp.
exampleJava: PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
commonMistakes: Comparing the wrong pair field in the heap comparator
Forgetting which pair slot is the priority and which is the payload
